Every Legend Kit in Riftbound's Radiance, Ranked

It's time for a comprehensive look at Radiance's Legend roster

By Zach Herwood-Mussen

|@TheZachkAttack
|

Published Oct 27, 2026

|

40 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Riftbound's fifth set Radiance hit shelves last week with 180 cards, three new mechanics, and nine new legends to build your decks around. Choosing your legend is the very first decision players make when deciding to conquer the rift, so I'll be breaking down each package: the Legend, Champion Units, and Signature Spell for each to help you decide what to build in the upcoming season of Riftbound.

Seraphine

Seraphine, Starry-Eyed Songstress

Seraphine is a Mind-Order (Blue-Yellow) Legend that reduces a spell's cost by two energy if you exhaust her and three friendly units. Cheaper spells in the domains with the strongest spells can make a huge difference, but needing three readied units is a steep cost. The first read of the deck looks like it wants to amass token recruit units like other decks in this color combination, but unlike Viktor it doesn't have easy access to spamming the board.

Exhausting units for a benefit is an interesting design to build a Legend around, as it gives additional benefit to holding when you aren't moving your units, but this means the deck has to be good at taking battlefields and amassing units before the legend comes online. I think she has a lot of competition for a color combo that already has strong strategies with Viktor and Leblanc. 

Seraphine, Not Alone

Seraphine's abilities need to be incredibly strong to justify five Energy and an Order Power for a one Might and unfortunately I don't think her card makes up for it. On an empty board, she is three Might across two units (a one Might Recruit and a buffed two Might Seraphine) with no way to conquer. On a developed board, Seraphine can strengthen a hold with enough other units, but this also shows her biggest flaw: your opponent can easily two-for-one your board by focusing on removing exhausted units that also drop Seraphine's Might.

It's difficult not to compare her to Azir, Sovereign, a card that costs the same for a readied four Might unit that can turn a developed board into a game-ending play. I think if Seraphine traded the on play wording for accelerate, she could have been an all-star on offense and defense. As she stands, I think the card is better in the binder than on the board.

Seraphine, Inspiring

The Mind Champion unit is Seraphin, Inspiring. At the cost of four energy and one mind power, you get a three might unit with disarm two which allows her to attack at a rate of five might at a contested battlefield. Although it's a solid statline, one power on a card that doesn't immediately impact the board is steep. Seraphine, Inspiring does have a secondary effect that allows you to draw one card when you exhaust three or more friendly units at the same time. 

Once your Seraphine Legend's ability is online, your blue Seraphine adds card draw to your discounted spells and we can start to see an engine forming. Letting blue Seraphine sit in the chosen Champion slot until you can take advantage of the draw is a solid strategy and it's not too difficult to get at least a card back from her, but it's a lot of effort to get a little bit of card draw.

Encore

Modal cards are almost always valuable and Encore has four modes to choose from to fit any situation you Might find yourself in. For three energy and one power of Mind or Order, you get two choices from: dealing two damage to a unit, creating two recruit tokens, giving two units plus one Might, or one card to hand from the top two of your deck. Encore covers quite a bit of ground, but the slow spell speed gives me a bit of pause. It's also a bit nerve-wracking that this is a card that does a lot of lifting but can still be Defy'd. 

In most situations, I think the best combination is putting two recruit tokens into play and drawing a card as the card effectively replaces itself and gets you two recruits. These two effects will be valuable at most points in the game, whether you have a board or not, but the other options could potentially tip the scales when trying to break a battlefield. Sadly, even with its modality I don't think Encore does enough on its own to make it really stand out as a signature spell. It makes the deck if you're already committed to Seraphine, but don't expect it to win games on the spot.

I think most of the Seraphine package is kept too safe to really make a splash. The other token-centered decks like Viktor, Azir, and Lilia importantly give you ways to play tokens, which I believe to be Seraphine's downfall. Unless she can consistently keep three units readied to reduce her spell costs, she's a blank Legend that would be better replaced by Viktor, and if you are able to keep the momentum and amount of units in play, you probably don't need her ability to tip the scales.


Rating: F - Whether it's about the climb or you just love boulders, this is a Sisyphean deck for only the die-hard fans.

Ekko

Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time

Ekko is a Mind Fury Legend with a set of paired abilities: the first ability pays one energy to empower him and the second ability spends that empowered status to reduce the cost of your next unit by two energy and one power, but gives that unit "kill me at end of turn". This means that Ekko has a two-turn rotation: the first to empower, then the second spends it, effectively paying a one energy tax for the hope that future turns can take advantage of it. 

On paper, this looks easy in early turns - going second you can play a two drop and empower him with no cost in tempo. The cost reduction is really powerful, being able to conserve ruins without paying power costs is potent alone, but the restriction of killing off the unit at end of turn limits it to powerful on play abilities or finding ways to 'blink' (removing the unit from play then replaying it), which means adding more hoops to the strategy overall. 

Ekko, Ingenious

Three energy and no power for a four Might unit is a great starting point, but give it ganking and a cost that's secretly an upside? Red Ekko has some very steep competition for the chosen Champion slot. Typically the three cost Champion unit is there to be played early, but I think this Ekko in the Champion slot can be a great boost to the deck to get more out of play effects, keep important pieces out of harm's way after they conquer, and, most importantly, to dodge the Legend's 'die at the end of the turn' clause. 

In other decks, Blue Ekko may not be as critical to the game plan as Pack of Wonders, but he does offer a similar amount of depth to get the most out of cheap units with powerful effects. Blue Ekko brings solid value to the toolbox while still being an impactful unit capable of taking points and beating down enemies. 

Ekko, Revolutionary

Ekko, Revolutionary is certainly a contender against Ekko, Ingenious. For five and a fury, you get a four Might (five Might when attacking) unit that enters ready which is a great starting point for a unit to quickly threaten a board state. In addition to this stat line, red Ekko has an action-speed ability that, at the cost of discarding one card and paying one energy and one fury power, 'blinks' him back to base. I believe being able to 'feint' battlefield attacks is an underutilized skill and something that will become increasingly valuable as the game progresses. 

Taking both battlefields for six and two fury is decidedly powerful, but it's also valuable to attack one battlefield to draw out interaction, then blink to dodge the interaction and attack the other battlefield. This can also be used defensively to send Ekko back to base for the follow up turn where he can attack again. In the Ekko deck, you also have access to the legend ability, which can reduce red Ekko's cost to three energy or four energy and a fury power to attack twice and dodge the 'kill at end of turn effect'. Outside of the Ekko deck, this card is still incredibly potent as a mid-game attacker that can fuel various Chaos-Fury strategies as well. The ceiling is incredibly high on this card and I expect him to make quite the wave in the upcoming meta.

Chronobreak

Chronobreak is a potentially board wide blink that requires you to pay two energy and one additional power for each unit you want to blink. At slow speed, it's hard to evaluate exactly how strong this card is. A second 'on play' effect from each of your more powerful units is good, but going beyond two unit choices starts to set you back multiple turns worth of runes. The cost of blinking a single unit is the same cost reduction the Ekko legend offers, so unless the repeated on play effects warrant it, I don't think decks will want to max out on copies of this card. 


It's simplicity, however, does mean that in the right circumstances this could fuel a potent combo, it is just entirely reliant on what you are able to blink with it. Firebrand Raider, for example, could help you blink your board for a second attack run by blinking all your units to base and having them enter play readied after Firebrand. Chronobreak has potential to be powerful, but it's kept largely in check by its timing restriction, which it needs for any semblance of balance.

Rating:B - There's definitely sauce here, but it's all thyme so far. Mind-Fury has a lot of technique built into its card pool and only time will tell if someone can bring it back together into a well-tuned masterpiece.

K'Sante

K'Sante, Pride of Nazumah

K'sante is a Calm-Body Legend with an ability that costs one energy and exhausts him to give a unit the text "I have assault equal to my shield this turn". In essence, this turns the units with high defensive outputs into offensive units that can take a point and then keep it secure. Like Ekko above, this means that you're paying a one energy tax on most turns to keep your offensive output high enough. This can turn your Stalwart Poros and Mutated Mousers into 3 Might units on offense or defense, but getting those units onto a battlefield early in the game hasn't been difficult historically. 

The issue I see with K'Sante is that he is trying to solve a problem that isn't there. The design of shield units is that they are stronger when holding, so they need access to a held battlefield to get the most value. K'Sante's power is helping your units conquer those held battlefields, but the game design has been 'take a battlefield on turn two or three, then layer shield units on top of it until you opponent gives up taking it'. Once the game is established, you're unlikely to commit low-cost shield cards to base, you'll use them to defend an already held battlefield and force your opponent to come to you. What is missing in the color set are units with powerful hold abilities that could use shield value as breakpoints, which K'Sante could turn into offensive units that force your opponent to engage on their turn. Currently, there just isn't enough to work with.

K'Sante, Courageous

K'Sante, Courageous is the type of unit that I would like to see access to. For five energy, the Orange K'Sante is a four Might unit with shield two with Accelerate and "when I hold, channel one rune". Accelerate helps turn him into an offensive card, but this does mean you're spending seven and an orange power on a six might attack. It's a lot of resources on an attack that feels slightly below rate and a trigger that would require him to survive two turns of combat (attacking on your turn and defending on your opponent's turn.

The hold trigger is strong, as the rune does not enter exhausted, but the accelerate feels like window dressing on a card that fits into other existing card pools. This gives Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman an eight might unit to plant on defense or a Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger on the opponent's turn to get an additional rune. My initial read is that he's good, I'm just not sure he's good enough to carry the deck.

K'Sante, Dauntless

Our calm K'Sante, is K'Sante, Dauntless: a four might unit for the cost of four energy and one calm power. K'Sante, Dauntless has shield one, making him a five might unit on defense, and the ability to double the shield value of a unit with him when he attacks or defends. Alone, this means he would be a six on offense with use of the K'Sante Legend or a six on defense all the time. 

With only shield one, I think a better use would be to pair the green K'Sante with another unit that has a higher shield count. Mutated Mouser, for example, becomes a five might defender next to him, but this also calls out the biggest flaw in the deck: Blue Sentinel, Disciple of Shen, and Shen, Kinkou are all incredible cards to pair with K'Sante that.. aren't in his colors. 

Ntofo Strikes

Ntofo Strikes might be the reason to play K'Sante. For two energy and a Calm or Body power, you get an action-speed spell that gives a friendly unit Shield two and then deals damage equal to the Shield value on the unit to an enemy unit. At minimum, this means plus two might and deal two damage, with the ability to scale upwards depending on the unit's base Shield value. Mutated Mouser going to a five might unit that deals four to any enemy unit is pretty strong and, with K'Sante's Legend ability you can use it on offense. Its versatility and low cost makes it worthwhile to run a full playset of, but without a beefy unit in play, I think it definitely loses some luster the further the game goes on.

Rating: D - I really want to love K'Sante, but I'm not sure the card pool has quite caught up with his particular brand yet. There's a great idea here with turning heavy shield units into attackers, but I don't think there are enough cards to take advantage of quite yet and there's simply better options in this color-pairing.

Orianna

Orianna, Lady of Clockwork

Orianna is a Calm-Mind Legend with the ability to pay one energy at the start of your main phase to make a friendly gear a unit gear with Might equal to its energy cost. This remains until she chooses another gear, so she can only ever animate one gear. Despite being another gear focused Legend in these colors, Orianna looks very different from Ornn and wants to play with a different suite of cards, especially gears with the new Deploy mechanic. Deploy lets you play gear to a battlefield, where they stay until an opponent holds there, which kills the gear. For Orianna, this means she can deploy a gear, then animate that gear on the following turn and either conquer if it was an empty battlefield or start a showdown with her gear if the opponent had units there. 

Orianna will be a synergy-focused deck that wants to take advantage of animating gears whenever she can to continually apply pressure while she does the typical Calm/Mind shenanigans. However, this does mean her strength depends on the value of the gears she can animate. It does give her a new axis to attack from, as she can play unassuming gears then animate one and send it into combat without committing very many resources. Her interesting playstyle means that players will be spending a lot of time trying to unlock her hidden potential.

Orianna, Exquisite

Orianna, Exquisite has the perfect stat line at three energy and no power for a four might unit with shield one. The downside is that she only deals combat damage when a gear is at her location. Since the Legend wants to play gears, this is barely a downside and pairing her with equipment gives you an over-statted unit that's hard to kick off a battlefield. 

Between deployed gears, equipment, and animated gear units, the calm Orianna will be the prime unit for her deck to push early battlefields and to fortify them with her even stronger defenses.

Orianna, Mechanical Marvel

There's not much to say about the mind Orianna. She's a five might unit for five energy that lets you pay one energy and one power less for a gear while she's at a battlefield. Ornn's Forge was a strong battlefield for gear decks, so I imagine that Orianna, Clockwork Marvel will find her position in decks. 

With her in the Champion slot, Orianna can send an animated gear in to take a battlefield, then play her and immediately start gaining the reduced costs, which is how I expect her to be played most of the time. 

The Ball

Conversely, there's a lot to be said about The Ball, Orianna's Signature Gear. For five energy and a Calm or Mind power, you get a gear with Deploy, Ganking, and whenever it's played or moves you can choose to draw one card or deal two damage to all enemy units at its location. The safest play pattern is putting The Ball at an empty battlefield, drawing a card, then animating it on the following turn to get a point and send it into the other battlefield (dealing two to everything there). This isn't a bad play pattern, but it is telegraphed to give your opponent plenty of opportunities to interact.

The opposite strategy is to send the ball at a fortified battlefield to weaken it, then send in another unit to break the battlefield and keep The Ball alive. There are enough decks in the game that wilt at 'two damage to everything here' that the strategy of developing a board then using The Ball to crack open a battlefield for your units is a devastating play. If The Ball reaches animation, it provides enough value that it should snowball your games, but I'm concerned that the number of ways to interact before it gets there might make this a difficult card to pin your hopes on.

Rating: C - I think Calm-Mind is a color combo that's always close to meta contention and rewards players with deep understanding of the game. Unlike Nasus, Orianna doesn't need to wait for the bird and can play a more aggressive start. The caveat, of course, is that the more prevalent gear decks become, the more common the main deck hate becomes, so you'll have to spend a lot of time learning to play against the decks that have the easiest games against you to survive. 

Evelynn

Evelynn, Agony's Embrace

Evelynn, Agony's Embrace is our Body-Chaos Legend and if you thought the art was spicy, wait until you read the text. Once per turn, when you play a card from facedown, Evelynn lets you draw a card, then if it is your turn, you discard one. While the clear gameplan here is to play your hidden cards on your turn, 'looting' as card selection is still really good since the cost is very low. You will need to take early control of a battlefield to get value out of her, but that's not too difficult in these colors thanks to strong control cards in chaos and powerful pump spells in orange.

The strength of Evelynn relies on the mind game and forcing your opponent to make bad trades. Card selection is strong enough that revealing hidden cards on your opponent's turn isn't bad, but this forces them to need to contest your hidden cards on their turn or let you get the clean draw. Forcing your opponent to play into your game and being able to circumvent their strategies with the cards already available, while also having powerful card selection, all of these factors lead me to believe that Evelynn will be a powerful legend in the upcoming season. 

Evelynn, Consuming

The first Evelynn Champion unit in the set is Evelynn, Consuming. This Epic-rarity Champion is five energy and a Body power for a five might unit with Ambush that readies and gains a might whenever you play a card from face down. For me, if a Champion unit costs a power I need it to impact the board immediately and ambush does allow this Evelynn to give a five might boost to a battlefield on defense. 


Her secondary ability is a little awkward: it's always relevant to give a might boost on top of playing a hidden card, but readying her implies you want to sidestep battlefields which she can't do easily. Ideally, you would play her on defense in the opponent's turn to avoid having to use the hidden card there, then move her back to base and flip the hidden card to have her ready at six might to attack the other battlefield. Despite this awkwardness, I think the card is strong in a similar, albeit weaker, way that Rengar, Trophy Hunter was. Keeping her face up in the chosen Champion slot so that you can always threaten a plus five boost in combat is a powerful deterrent. 

Evelynn, In Control

Our rare Champion unit in Radiance is Evelynn, In Control. For four energy and a chaos power, the chaos Evelynn has four might and Disarm, allowing her to fight on offense at a contested battlefield for five might. Her secondary ability, however, makes me want to keep her in the chosen Champion slot as a pure defender. When she holds, if you control a facedown card at her location she scores one additional point. Point scorers can be incredibly impactful, even though this one has a rather difficult hoop to jump through. In games where you're already ahead, it will be easy to press on the gas with her at an overly defended point. 

In more back-and-forth games, Evelynn can be used to apply pressure that forces the opponent to spend resources to remove her or your lock on a point. I think playing exactly one copy in the chosen Champion slot so that you can threaten the extra point on the right turn could be the play to force the all-in from the opponent, but orange Evelynn might be too good to not have access to at every stage of the game.

Last Caress

Last Caress is Evelynn's signature spell and it is powerful. For two energy and a body or chaos power, this reaction-speed spell lets you play your next unit anywhere and when you do, you buff it. This includes your hidden units, so you can play this on your opponent's turn, then flip up a hidden card and move it to the other battlefield. On your turn, transforming any unit in the deck into an orange Rengar for two and a power is a pretty bold move, but the added benefit of being able to do this on your opponents turn to make a free battlefield contested makes this incredible. 

Free conquers that turn into holds was already a potent play with Rengar, but being able to use it for a multitude of other units gives me plenty of hesitation to commit any deploy gear.

Rating: B - I think Evelynn has a lot of potential with a very deep card pool. The stronger players will make this deck a fearsome dream-killer as it requires a bit of finesse to play correctly. My favorite part of the deck, however, is that it doesn't want Aurora and that's going to be enough of a reason for me to jam this deck from day one onwards.

Ziggs

Ziggs, Hexplosives Expert

Our Chaos Fury Legend is the bombastic Yordle himself, Ziggs. Ziggs has an activated ability that costs one energy and one power to deploy a Bomb gear to a battlefield. When that bomb dies, whether your opponent holds the battlefield or you manage to kill the gear yourself, it can deal two damage to a unit at that location then blows up every other Bomb at the battlefield. The set also includes a decent amount of ways to create Bombs, so you can flood the board with bombs to keep your opponent from any quick conquers early in the game.

Ziggs aims to play a solid control strategy that is common to Chaos, but exchanges the tempo of temporarily removing threats with completely blowing up the units. In a typical game of Riftbound, players are creating trades on battlefields with units with the limiting factor being how many cards you have access to. This deck offers a new mental game by being able to stack bombs on battlefields the Ziggs player doesn't control, which increases the value of their cards since they can spend fewer on removing threats. The opponent now has to decide to sacrifice their units knowing they can't hold onto battlefields or holding back and potentially allowing the Ziggs to stack bombs higher to take out larger threats.

The largest limiter on Ziggs is the energy cost of his ability. Ideally, you can set up scenarios where you're layering bombs every turn, but that means losing a rune every turn. Seals can be a massive game changer here, especially if a detonate build appears that turns late-game Seals into card draw into more threats. 

Ziggs, Short-Fused

The epic Champion unit for Ziggs is the Fury card Ziggs, Short-Fused. At five energy and a Fury power for five might, this card isn't cheap but can have an immediate impact on the board. He adds a bomb to a battlefield on play, then has a passive ability that increases the damage gears deal by one. With zero other investments, this means that red Ziggs can plant a bomb on a battlefield an opponent holds, then deal three damage to the unit there when the bomb pops on your opponent's turn. When paired with the Ziggs legend ability, this increases to six damage which is enough to pop a large majority of units! 

Ziggs, Short-Fused seems strong since he can immediately offer a tempo swing, but is a huge threat if you're not winning the game outright. There's some interesting synergies outside Bomb tokens with cards like Iron Ballista, although this starts to veer into win-more territory if it works. He'll likely be planted at base, keeping him safe from harm, while you toss bombs and force your opponent off points. Pack one in your chosen Champion slot to terrify your opponent into playing slow while you set up and push ahead.

Ziggs, Explosive

Ziggs, Explosive is our rare Chaos Champion unit. A cost of four energy and no power cost for four might is close to our gold standard, but no way to impact the board unless he's played defending a battlefield gives me pause. Purple Ziggs has an activated ability to exhaust him and pay one energy to deploy a bomb, but since he can't do that on the turn he's played you need to already have a bomb in place to get full value.

The upside to this is that a Ziggs, Explosive with a bomb at his location can defend at an assumed total of eight might! When he defends, he can pop a bomb to gain two might, putting him to six might total, and since the bomb popped you can also deal two damage to one of the attackers. Being able to reach PG Yi levels of defense looks promising, especially in a color that usually struggles with keeping strong defenders in play, but unless you have enough ways to plant bombs, I don't think Ziggs, Explosive can be justified in the deck.

Hexplosive Minefield

Ziggs's signature card is Hexplosive Minefield, a card that can do nothing, everything, but most of the time something. For two energy and a Chaos or Fury power, Hexplosive Minefield is an action speed spell that kills any number of bomb tokens, then replays that many bomb tokens at the end the of turn. The obvious caveat here is that the card needs a number of bombs to played at all and ideally those bomb explosions need to accomplish something. 

Assuming you can get roughly three bombs at a battlefield, the existence of the card can make most opponents hesitate at running in as you can just pop the bombs in the showdown and potentially plant them in a more disastrous spot. Alternatively, you can use this on your turn to soften a battlefield for a conquer, then replant the bombs at the opposing battlefield and potentially wipe your opponent off the board entirely. 

Because Hexplosive Minefield requires so much investment from other cards and abilities, it's hard to estimate just how valuable the card will be in the deck. Seeing one per game should be more than enough to turn the tide of a game, but seeing additional copies in hand instead of impactful units seems terrible. In my opinion, keep two copies in the deck and pitch the first one you see in an opening hand without worry. 

Rating: B - Off card pool alone, you can expect Ziggs to show up at Nexus Nights or even larger events. He can play deeper into the tempo strategies that his color combo already excels at while simultaneously being a harder deck to play against than other tempo strategies. A lot of his strength comes from how effective you are with his bomb placement, however, as even a single dud explosion could tip the tempo against him. The biggest concern I have for Ziggs is opponents being able to stack deflect or 'untargetable' effects, as this is already an issue for Chaos decks. I expect that Ziggs will be able to satchel charge his way over the competition, but I'd recommend waiting for the professionals to perfect the list before bringing it to a skirmish. 

Jarvan IV

Jarvan IV, Exemplar of Demacia

Jarvan IV, heir apparent to the Demacian throne, is Radiance's Body-Order legend ("a fitting combination for a tyrant playing at king" - Sylas). 

Jarvan's ability allows you to pay a power and exhaust him when a deploy gear is played to a battlefield to move a friendly unit there. While Jarvan has a tighter focus than Orianna, the trade of getting movement abilities in a domain combination that struggles to maintain tempo. Being able to play a high cost unit, then deploy a gear to immediately threaten the board. This also allows you to counter-attack from a held battlefield, as Jarvan moves the unit and doesn't need ganking to do so. 

The biggest downside of Jarvan is needing a steady amount of deploy gears to keep using his ability and Radiance only introduces a few playable gears for Jarvan's domains. I think this will have a big impact on how he shows up at the table, but also gives Riot plenty of space to improve him with better cards in the future. 

Jarvan IV, Royal Heir

Jarvan IV, Royal Heir is the rare Order Champion unit costing a staggering seven energy and one Order power. For that cost, you're getting a seven might unit with assault one, Tank, and the ability to bring a friendly unit with him when he attacks. This means he can threaten a variable amount of might when attacking, with a minimum of eight might if he attacks alone. Usually I would find these cards unplayable as there is no on-card way to immediately impact play, but when combined with a cheap deploy gear, Jarvan IV can suddenly bring enough might to take out Baron!

When everything is working, the Order Jarvan IV is a massive threat and I find that makes them perfect in the chosen Champion slot: you can wait for the right turn to play him with a deploy gear from hand to quickly change the tempo of the game. Like all high-cost units, however, he falls into the trap of being easily removed via cards like Star-crossed. This not only tempos your unit, but also potentially throws away your deploy gear if you use it to contest an already held battlefield. At his best, this Jarvan is fantastic and at his worst his nigh-unplayable.

Jarvan IV, Martial Paragon

Opposite the Order Jarvan is Jarvan IV, Martial Paragon the Epic Body Champion Unit. Martial Paragon costs four and one Body energy for a four might unit that give your deploy gear action speed. When this Jarvan conquers a battlefield where you planted a deploy gear, you can channel one rune exhausted as a way to help offset the Legend ability's cost. As any deploy gear in the deck will telegraph your plays, being able to play them at action speed during an opponent's showdown gives the deck a decent amount of versatility. A powerful play would be putting the Body Jarvan at a battlefield to defend as a way to force your opponent to attack the other battlefield, then playing a deploy gear mid-shown to move him over to defend that battlefield as well. It's a few more hoops than just playing Ride the Wind, but it synergizes well with Jarvan's kit overall and gives more upside to keeping the loop going.

The problem I see with Martial Paragon is that, like the Legend, you don't have enough strong deploy gear to build around this. It will be something powerful the deck does occasionally, but focusing on this particular interaction might be reserved for playing the deck on December 26. There are too many ways for your opponent to play around, either through removal or just being able to counter obvious plays.

Demacian Standard

The final piece of Jarvan IV's kit is his signature card, Demacian Standard, which is thankfully a deploy gear! As a League of Legends player, the flavor of being able to drop the Standard and 'pull' a Jarvan IV unit to the location is unparalleled, but Demacian Standard is also easily the best card in his kit. For two energy and a Body or Order power, Demacian Standard deploys to a battlefield and grants one of your attackers there plus two might for the turn. At a combined cost of two energy and two power, you can send a unit to a contested battlefield with the ability to fight at a higher weight class thanks to the might boost, which is pretty strong for its cost. 

Additionally, whenever you hold the battlefield where Demacian Standard is deployed, you can return it to hand and re-drop it at the other battlefield to keep the wreckage going!

At most stages of the game, this card will immediately impact the board and is very difficult for your opponent to interact with (unless we see more dedicated gear hate in the main board). The additional might is crucial to those small, early game units that allows them to trade or potentially conquer larger units. Your opponent then has a heavy incentive to retake that battlefield to keep you from returning the Standard to hand, which also lets you attack and gain the might boost over and over again.

Rating: C - Looking at only his cards, Jarvan IV feels like a contender. When you start to build the deck, however, it becomes apparent that there just aren't enough cards to support him yet. The very slim offerings for deploy gear mean that you have to max out on any that seem playable at all, while also playing all of the tried-and-true cards that Body needs to be at the table with Chaos. I really really want to like Jarvan IV, and I do, but I'll be keeping him in the binder until I see what set six gives us in the form of deploy gears.

Riven

Riven, the Exile

Our 'fated to be Tier 1' Calm-Chaos Legend is Riven, the Exile. Riven's Legend has the easiest ability to understand in Radiance: your units that enter play at a battlefield you control enter readied. Being able to play a Stellacorn readied at a battlefield, then move it back to base to draw one is probably enough to make Riven a meta-contender already, but there's a lot of utility wrapped into this simple text.

While Riven is focused entirely on holding onto a battlefield to get the most value, creating openings is what Calm-Chaos does. While the most face-up combo with Riven is being able to 'snipe' with Caitlyn the turn she comes into play, any unit with Ganking becomes a great threat when utilizing the 'readied on play' state Riven grants.

Riven, Broken Blade

Riven, Broken Blade is a Calm Unit that costs four energy, four might, and a set of abilities that trigger when she becomes exhausted. Each time she's exhausted she can choose to either: buff herself, spend her buff to stun an enemy unit, or spend her buff to ready herself. Her statline is solid for a champion unit, especially when considering she can reach five might if she uses the first exhaust trigger to buff herself, but the hoops feel a bit arbitrary. With no keywords, the most common strategies with her take two turns: play her to a battlefield, move back to base to buff, then be able to spend the buff attacking on the following turn or play her to base, then attack as a five might on the following turn.

The card reads as powerful, especially if she is readied multiple times in a turn, but Calm-Chaos is not in need of turn two/three powerful plays. In my opinion, she might find a better home in an Akali deck that can use the Legend ability to get two exhaust triggers, effectively allowing Riven to set up stunned enemies every turn to neutralize the opponent's ability to hold battlefields. 

Riven, Deserter

Riven, Deserter is the Epic Chaos Champion unit for the Riven kit. For five energy and a Chaos power, this Riven has five might and a pair of potent effects. Her first effect is a trigger that grants her one might whenever another friendly unit becomes exhausted, while the second effect lets her exhaust a friendly unit to ready a unit once per turn. Combining these two effects lets you play her from hand to base, then ready and attack at six might, a break point for most of the mid-game units. 


Like the lower rarity version, this Riven unit looks like it's trying to solve something that the Domains weren't struggling with. The upside here is that older Calm - Chaos decks were reaching these might breakpoints with a four might unit and Discipline. Riven, Deserter can accomplish the same amount as long as there is already a friendly readied unit to exhaust, so it's possible to hit higher break points with the Discipline backup. I like the design of this Riven that wants to be played at base instead of a held battlefield to take advantage of the heavy attack, but for an Epic Champion Unit it feels a bit basic.

Blade of the Exile

The card that brings the whole kit together is Riven's signature card, a gear named Blade of the Exile. The reforged blade of Riven is an equipment that costs three energy and a Calm or Chaos power, with an equip cost of a power or exhausting a friendly unit. For this cost, Blade of the Exile grants the equipped unit ganking and an additional three might! The Ganking keyword was the missing piece of the puzzle, as now you can use those readied units at battlefields to attack the enemy battlefield and the plus three might will get over most units and at least one pump spell. 

The alternative equip cost is fairly important, too, as this is what helps push Blade of the Exile above Boots of Swiftness. Riven has no trouble guaranteeing readied units, especially those that will remain at a battlefield to defend and don't need the readied status. In a domain combination that is usually Power hungry, being able to reduce these inefficiencies with cards like Blade of the Exile frees up space that players usually try to fill with seals. 

Rating: A - I think Riven has the best opportunity to be a meta contender out of any of the Radiance Legends. A big part of this is the domain combination and the amount of power that comes from abusing Stellacorn draw, but the biggest advantage for most players is that the gameplay loops are simplified for Riven. The most common complaint I saw when players were first starting to play Irelia was that the mechanical plays were taxing to learn. Riven makes this easier by setting up the puzzle: your units are readied, but can't get directly to the enemy; the deckbuilding process then helps players solve this puzzle and reward them for sticking to or adapting their gameplan. 

The tradeoff for this simplicity is that there aren't as many interesting options for the deck. The ganking and Caitlyn tricks are neat, but they're party tricks in a sea of decks designed to block attacks at any angle. The deck most likely to be built out of this will use Heron to slow down aggressive strategies, then use the readied units to eke out advantage over the course of the game. It won't be flashy and, given how the end of Vendetta meta looked, I wouldn't be surprised to see some of the cards hit by banlist before Legacy.

Mordekaiser

Mordekaiser, Iron Revenant

Mordekaiser is our final Legend in Radiance and he's wielding the Noxian Fury-Order combination. Mordekaiser's ability requires you to exhaust him and banish a unit or gear from your trash to get a power you can only spend on playing gears or units. At first read, it's a simple resource generation with a hoop to jump through, but I think the deck has more nuance than this.

While most early discussion on Mordekaiser focused on finding discard or Burn outlets, I think the natural flow of the game will fill the trash. Presenting a held battlefield on turn two leads to your opponent deciding to counter-attack to remove your unit, potentially giving you the resource, or going to the free battlefield to avoid combat. This axis gives you a new way to play, where you force your opponent to engage with you so that you can efficiently play bigger threats across turns. 

This best way to utilize this gained efficiency is through the use of Accelerated units. Units with Accelerate can pay an additional one energy and one power of their domain to be played ready, so Mordekaiser's power generation can be used to create immediate threats that, when they die, fuel the next line of soldiers ready to charge up the battlefield.

Mordekaiser, Twice Slain

Mordekaiser, Twice Slain, the dominator of pre-rifts everywhere, costs seven energy and a Fury power or eight energy and two Fury to accelerate him. He has five might and assault three, allowing him to fight at eight might when attacking a battlefield. Mordekaiser also has the ability to cheat death once per turn by killing a friendly unit, exhausting him, and sending him back to base. 

This makes for a terrifying late-game unit that can fight most units on equal footing and sacrifice a small unit to keep harassing the opponent. Although he has a heavy cost, especially when accelerated, the legend offsets this a bit and the exchange is worth being able to fight off most battlefields. There is a devastating strategy here of taking a battlefield and forcing your opponent to kill him, only to send him back to base to do it again the following turn. When paired with relevant deathknell effects, you make it very difficult for your opponent to cleanly reduce your board presence. As long as you can keep up populating the board with units, this Mordekaiser will happily sit in the deck at max copies to fight off even the hardiest of opponents.

Mordekaiser, Dominating

If you thought the rare version was powerful, the Epic version of Mordekaiser is even more terrifying. At a massive nine energy and two Order power, Mordekaiser, Dominating is an eight might unit that lets you discard a card to kill a unit or gear whenever he is played or attacks. At one more energy than Harnessed Dragon, you get a more powerful unit that can take over the game on his own.

Like every card in this cost range, being able to stick a nine drop should be enough to win the game, but there are so many ways to nullify this that it's hard to be too excited. Mordekaiser, Dominating always does something on play, which is great, but spending your whole turn on a single pop, then watching the opponent spend four energy to kill him will be rough. If you're planning on playing Mordekaiser, the best strategy will be to plant one of these in the Chosen Champion slot and wait for an opening.

Realm of Death

Outside of Overnumbers (sorry, nothing beats Aphelios), Mordekaiser's signature spell, Realm of Death, is my favorite card by a very large margin. For two energy and a Fury or Order power, realm of death reduces an enemy unit's might by two and increases a friendly unit's might by two for the turn, then has the two units deal damage to each other. This is a fight spell, like Challenge or Rampage, but now accessible in Fury and Order domains.

Realm of Death is almost the most efficient fight spell we've seen so far, with a wider range of threat when compared to the others. Challenge can be used to trade any unit into its might or lower, say for example a two might unit that trades into a two might unit or kills a one might unit. If you pay the additional cost, Rampage adds two might to your unit, so now with our example unit we can trade into a four might unit or kill anything at three might or lower. Realm of Death spreads the math more with the two up/two down: our two might unit can trade into a six might unit, or kill anything at five or less. 

Knowing this math helps our deckbuilding as we can lay out how to handle any threatening unit in the game and knowing how to achieve your break points can win more games than just playing busted cards.

Rating: C This one might be influenced by my own bias, but I think Mordekaiser has quite a bit of staying power. Power costs have been a limiting factor on Fury-Order's ability to play relevant cards every turn and I think even the mental game of your opponent having to choose to give you points or value on impactful turns looks good. I don't think Mordekaiser can reach the same heights as other decks without Chaos or Mind, but I think it could be a local level meta slayer for those that dedicate themselves to the Noxii chieftain.

Every Legend with a resource generation loop has found its way to day two at a higher tournament, so I won't be surprised until I see him on coverage (and then I'll be super excited). Mordekaiser's simple design will continue to be viable in future sets as units and gears become more powerful with time, especially given that Legacy's design should give even more Noxian flare to the domain combo. I'll be dedicating my time in the meta to Sahn-Uzal trying to uncover the best strategies to overwhelm the opponents.

With that, we've ranked every new Legend kit arriving in Radiance! The set looks like a lot of fun, especially after playing it in pre-rift and in the few days since release, but outside of Mordekaiser I'm actually looking forward to putting new cards into older decks to see how much strength they've gained. Rumble looks particularly spicy and Irelia looks like she could be even more powerful than she has been in the past. 

No matter the power level, I'll be cracking packs in the upcoming weeks looking for that beautiful overnumbered Mordekaiser. I'm a HUGE sucker for Sahn-Uzal, as well as the Heartsteel cards! There's a lot to love in this set and I can't wait to get my decks built and battling on the rift.

Top 5 Best Pokémon TCG Cards From Delta Reign

Rayquaza is amazing, but have you seen this spicy bird?

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Oct 27, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Hello everyone! Delta Reign is almost here and with the new expansion we have some new cards to talk about! This set does introduce the new split Stadium mechanic which pushes for stronger Stadiums at the cost of having to play both halves of the Stadiums from your hand, and outside of these there are a bunch of strong cards!

The Best Cards From Delta Reign

Honorable Mention

Aarune is a spiritual reprint of Scott from EX Emerald, which saw a bunch of play back in the mid 2000s. Aarune is a very slow card; using your Supporter for turn to only find other Supporters and Stadiums is generally very weak in the Pokémon TCG, but if a deck is intending to be slow then Aarune can be a very strong partner for it. Slower control decks generally rely heavily on Supporter cards for their strongest effects, and since you can find Aarune from another Aarune, the best way to use this card will likely be from chaining them together. Another aspect of Aarune is that you can use it alongside the new split Stadiums, making them significantly easier to put in play. Aarune is very slow and will be unlikely to be played in normal attacking decks, but has potential in slower, more controlling lists.

#5 Tasty Rice Ball

Jumbo Ice Cream has seen a bunch of play in slower control decks such as Crustle and Kangaskhan/Boufallant, and Tasty Rice Ball is a very similar card. The first Tasty Rice Ball only heals 30 from your active Pokémon, but  each subsequent Tasty Rice Ball heals an additional 30, with the final Tasty Rice Ball healing 120 damage. If you use all four Tasty Rice Ball throughout the game you heal 300 damage, and while this is less than the 320 you would heal from Jumbo Ice Creams, you can use Tasty Rice Ball while your active Pokémon has less than three Energy attached. I'm not currently expecting Tasty Rice Ball to surpass Jumbo Ice Cream, but I think it could supplement it for additional healing.

#4 Adventuring Lantern

Earthen Vessel was one of the strongest cards in the format for a long time, and while Adventuring Lantern is not as good as Earthen Vessel was, it's still a very strong card. Many decks want access to Energy, and while you can only use Earthen Vessel for Fire and Lightning Energy, it's still a powerful card. Any deck that uses either type of Energy can likely consider including Adventuring Lantern, as the additional type can be used for Colorless Energy costs. Many decks also use Crispin and can use the additional type to fuel the acceleration effect on Crispin, and I also believe that Adventuring Lantern will be combined with the next card on this list.

#3 Mega Rayquaza ex

Mega Rayquaza ex is the headliner of this set and I think it has a ton of competitive potential. It's a 280 Basic Pokémon, and has the Roar of the Ruler ability that lets you look at the top four cards of your deck and attach a Basic Energy you find there to it, then Storm Emeralda does 50 damage for each Fire and Lightning Energy on your board. You do need to get to six and sometimes seven Energy in play to take big knockouts, but you can use Ethan's Ho-Oh ex's Golden Flame ability to attach extra Energy every turn and fuel Storm Emeralda. Outside of that, you can also use Crispin and multiple Mega Rayquaza, alongside Area Zero Underdepths to fuel Energy in play, and I could see Storm Emeralda quickly ramping to a point where it's taking one-hit knockouts on anything. I would expect this deck to play similarly to the current Basic Box decks, and I imagine they will include the number one card on this list as well!

#2 Legendary Pyroduct

There are a few Legendary Stadiums in this expansion, but I think the strongest one is Legendary Pyroduct. Shutting off the abilities of all evolution Pokémon is very powerful and will likely be a mainstay at some point in its lifetime. Currently, it turns off the Powerful Hand abilities of the Alakazam line, Run Away Draw from Dudunsparce, Drakloak's Recon Directive and Crustle's Mysterious Rock Inn, as well as shutting off a number of other decks in the metagame. The biggest downside of this card is that the two halves of the Stadiums are difficult to piece together, putting a big roadblock in place for playing it early. Given how powerful the effect of this card is, I believe it'll see competitive play even though it's very difficult to put into play.

#1 Talonflame ex

One of the strongest cards in the format currently is Mega Kangaskhan ex. Many decks rely on the Run Errand ability to draw tons of cards, and it also cleanly activates the Exciting Dive ability on this Talonflame ex, allowing you to put it directly into play. It has 280 HP, free retreat and for two Energy it can use Talon Hunt, which does 150 and searches your deck for two cards and adds them to your hand. This is a fantastic card for any big basic deck as it's a very strong two-Prize attacker in the early game. You set up your hand with Talon Hunt, and even facilitate a later Legendary Pyroduct alongside a Judge to disrupt any evolution deck, or just build up an attacker next turn. I would expect Talonflame ex to be slotted into many of the various big basic decks in the format and be used as a strong two-Prize attacker.

Clone Your Way to Victory With Reality Fracture's Uldaros Theorix in Commander

Counting to six has never been easier.

By Tyler Berger

|

Published Oct 27, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Commander Bestiary

Even in the Echoverse, the Commander Bestiary is here to give you all the best deck guides! We've returned with another of Hexhaven's sphinx leaders: Uldaros Theorix! 

The Founder of Theorix

In Jace's Echoverse, the Strixhaven school is twisted into Hexhaven, a military school. Uldaros Theorix is the founder of the Theorix School of Esoteric Mathematics, an echo of Strixhaven's Quandrix school. He wears chains of equations and bends reality with his mathematic magic

Uldaros Theorix simplifies its incredible math spells to some basic addition: just count to six! When Uldaros enters, if you cast him, you'll exile up to one nonland card of each card type from your graveyard. Then, you can copy those cards, up to a total mana value of six. For example, you could exile one creature that costs four and a sorcery that costs two, and copy them both for free. 

With a stocked graveyard, casting your commander nets you a ton of value, paying back the six mana you invested into Uldaros. That said, Uldaros is a bit slow at six mana, but that's less of a problem than you might think. You'll need a graveyard loaded with different card types before Uldaros is worth casting, so you can focus on that before you worry about casting your commander. The other issue is those four words: "if you cast him". 

You can't abuse Uldaros's ability using cards like Reanimate or Ghostly Flicker. There are still some ways to bend the rules in your favor with clone effects, which we'll be featuring heavily today.

Esoteric Mathematics (But With Clones)

Today's deck will be centered on a clone strategy, as it's one of the only ways to take full advantage of Uldaros Theorix's abilities. When Uldaros exiles a card and copies it, you still cast that copy, despite not paying the mana cost. If you do this with a clone like, well, Clone, you can have it enter as a copy of Uldaros. Your Clone will die to the legend rule, but its ability will still resolve – and it will remember that you cast that object, regardless of the fact that its name changed or that it died. That'll get you another Uldaros trigger, which you can keep using on clone cards, while getting some additional spells each time you do this. 

Another cool idea for Uldaros is as a Jace deck. Reality Fracture brought the Empower Jace mechanic (such as on Way of the Mind Sculptor), which puts extra loyalty counters on a Jace token you control, and creates a simple Jace token if you don't already have one. Now, since Uldaros's ability exiles the original card, any permanents you copy will enter as tokens. You can have Uldaros exile a regular Jace planeswalker like Jace, Reality Sculptor, creating a token copy – thus allowing your Empower Jace cards to work with a "real" planeswalker! Empower will boost your Jace's loyalty faster than anyone will be prepared for, letting you pop a planeswalker ultimate out of nowhere.

Infinite Combos, Infinite Possibilities

This is a self-mill deck, so you knew you'd see Thassa's Oracle rear its fishy head. While today's deck is going for a more "honest" self-mill win, the power of Thassa's Oracle can't be denied, especially when combined with Demonic Consultation or Tainted Pact to exile your whole library.

There are also some combos using more fair pieces. I mentioned Singularity Rupture in the previous section: a board wipe that can also turbocharge your graveyard. An effect like that paired with Riverchurn Monument will mill your opponents out on the spot, and the monument is an otherwise useful self-mill card in the meantime. While today's deck is going to lean closer to Bracket 2, you can very easily push it into a higher bracket by including these kinds of cards together. They'll be good cards on their own, while having a chance to get a surprise combo win. 

How to Play Uldaros Theorix in Commander

Your first priority is to get mana on the board and cards in your graveyard. Repeatable self-mill engines like Ripples of Undeath and Hedron Crab are at their best here, letting you passively build a graveyard while doing other things. You can also play out mana sources like Deranged Assistant and The Warring Triad to pull double duty. Don't be afraid to cast cards like Frantic Search early to ensure your land drops – you'll get more mileage out of that card from the graveyard anyway.

You'll want a graveyard with multiple clones and self-mill effects before you cast Uldaros. The various clones all have something to offer. Low cost ones like Phantasmal Image are great, because Uldaros gets an additional four mana value to copy on top of the clone. Waxen Shapethief is a mostly normal clone, but I like that it puts itself in the graveyard if you want. Spark Double and Sakashima of a Thousand Faces are your best clones, because they let you cheat the legend rule in one way or another. Now, each of your Uldaros clones will stay in play for a potentially lethal attack – just in case your primary plan doesn't work out.

Once your graveyard is filled up, have Uldaros copy a clone like Waxen Shapethief along with a spell like Glimpse the Unthinkable. Make sure to stack them so your self-mill happens first. That way, the Clever Impersonator cloning Uldaros will have even more cards to choose from. Keep repeating this sequence, making sure to add any cards to get the most of Uldaros's six mana value of free spells. Cards like Ancestral Vision and Lotus Bloom can be included without adding to the total mana value. 

Just remember, Uldaros Theorix can only copy cards of different types – no doubling up on instants, for example. This deck has more creatures and instants than the other types, but there's also plenty of sorceries and artifacts, and a couple of enchantments, to make the most of Uldaros's ability. 

If you can keep the sequence of clones and self-mill repeating, you'll run your library out in no time. That's where your win conditions come in: Laboratory Maniac and Jace, Wielder of Mysteries. You can certainly use the aforementioned Thassa's Oracle in a higher bracket deck, too – that one's even more efficient and difficult to interact with. If your plan comes across an obstacle like Bojuka Bog hitting your win conditions, you have emergency buttons with Perpetual Timepiece and Paradox Shaper to recycle some key cards.

Things won't always go according to plan, so we're planning for the plan to whiff sometimes. We're playing several ways to cast Uldaros again, getting another trigger and keep those wheels spinning. Release to the Wind exiles Uldaros and lets you cast him again for free, even on a future turn if you prefer. Portal of Sanctuary is a repeatable bounce effect for Uldaros, and works great with Baleful Strix too. Snap is unassuming as a simple way to bounce Uldaros to your hand, but effects like this and Frantic Search untapping your lands are extremely powerful when you get them for free with Uldaros's ability. 

These kinds of effects help with your secondary gameplan – smacking your opponents with a huge sphinx. If the Laboratory Maniac win is somehow off the table, remember that Uldaros is simply a pile of card advantage. It might not win immediately, but casting your 5/5 flying sphinx and getting Fact or Fiction, Animate Dead, Lotus Petal, and Profane Tutor for free seems pretty good too! Your pile of clone effects can always copy other powerful effects on the board, so you can match the best cards being played against you.

I love putting together a big engine and setting it in motion, and this deck does exactly that. Uldaros Theorix is truly showing what theoretical mathematics can do when applied to a Commander deck!

Thanks for joining us for this edition of the Commander Bestiary! We have many more entries from Reality Fracture to check out, including the other Elder Sphinx legends! Buyer's Guide to Pokémon TCG: Delta Reign

Tracking down Rayquaza? You'll need an air-tight plan.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 22, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Pokémon's 30th Celebration set release has come, and it has gone. And while there's going to be plenty of 30th Celebration continually printed and released over the months to come heading into the holidays, the Pokémon world moves faster than a Mega Beedrill under Tailwind. In other words, while fans are still salivating about RGB Mews, the world is still turning, and Delta Reign is about to release.

Yes, the newest Pokémon set is almost here, just a little more than a month after the most-anticipated Pokémon release in history. It's a tough act to follow, but a pretty good way to do it is to put one of the game's most popular mascots at the front of the set, and that's exactly what Delta Reign is doing with Mega Rayquaza ex. One of the most iconic Pokémon in the franchise and one with a special place in the TCG's lore, Rayquaza guarantees at least one big hit at the top end of the upcoming set, which we don't yet have a full product list for.

Still, players and collectors are already eagerly anticipating the Nov. 6 release date for Delta Reign. Here's everything we know that's coming with the set.

Based on the Japanese set Storm Emeralda, Delta Reign has a few unique things going for it as the successor to 30th Celebration. For starters, the Rayquaza focus puts it in a tiny subset of Pokémon releases over the years, and the excitement around it has already driven up the price of multiple older printings of Rayquaza.

The set also introduces new Mega Evolution Pokémon to the TCG, as well as a new mechanic called a "Legendary Stadium." Each Legendary Stadium is made of two matching Stadium cards that are played together to put the Legendary Stadium in play. Delta Reign packs that contain a Legendary Stadium will come with both halves of the card, so no wild chases for that other half to complete the shared art.

Most of the products for Delta Reign will be available simultaneously on Nov. 6. Here's how they break down.

Elite Trainer Boxes

Contents:

  • 9 booster packs.
  • Foil Kyogre promo.
  • 65 sleeves.
  • 45 Energy cards.
  • Dice, coins, dividers.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $105.
  • Price per pack: $11.50.

The crown jewel of most Pokémon releases, Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) for Delta Reign will be available on Nov. 6 and come with the usual assortment of game pieces as well as nine booster packs.

With ETBs going for just over $100 on pre-sale, that works out to just over $11 per pack for a chance to chase that Rayquaza. ETBs are often seen as the best sealed product from a given release to hold onto long-term, which can often drive up the Market Price just like demand for the theoretical cards inside those packs do. That said, we've seen so many waves of printings for current sets that we can probably expect the ETB price to slide down some in the weeks after release.

Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Boxes

Contents:

  • 11 booster packs.
  • Foil Kyogre promo with stamp.
  • 65 sleeves.
  • 45 Energy cards.
  • Dice, coins, dividers.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $350.
  • Price per pack: $27.

The Pokémon Center is the official online portal for purchasing Pokémon products, which often comes with various markings that designate them as Pokémon Center-exclusives. This always causes a multiplier to the box's value, and we've seen some very expensive Pokémon Center ETBs over the years.

It can be hard to nail down the price of Pokémon Center boxes for a few months, but in this case, we have a nice amount of data to work with, and more than a handful currently for sale at the same price point. The Pokémon Center-exclusive versions of the Delta Reign Elite Trainer Boxes are currently listing for right around $300 right now.

These work out to a very expensive cost per pack, but keep in mind that these are very much considered a Sealed collector's item and are rarely cracked.

Delta Reign Build & Battle Box

Contents: 

  • A 40-card ready-to-play deck, including 1 of 4 unique foil promo cards.
  • 4 Pokémon booster packs.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $68.
  • Price per pack: $17.

Live listings for this one are actually trending lower at a quick rate right now, but this product that can either be had at the Prerelease or later in stores. It comes with a ready-to-play 40-card deck that you can use in a Prerelease event at a store or keep to play at home, as well as four booster packs. The Build and Battle boxes are also popular for the promos they come with. In the case of Delta Reign, you're able to receive one of either Masquerain, Magmortar, Enamorus, or Kommo-o.

While the current price of around $68 puts the price per pack here up to almost $17 a pack, that doesn't include the promo – plus there's a lot of value in having a deck ready to play out of the box. 40-card decks aren't legal in Standard play, but it's great for all the Pokémon games that take place on a kitchen table, a bedroom floor, or a lunchroom. 

Booster Boxes

Contents:

  • 36 booster packs.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $240.
  • Price per pack: $6.50.

If you want to go big, try and find a full booster box of Delta Reign. These boxes aren't as popular with most buyers in part due to their high upfront price tag, and in part because they simply don't look as nice when displayed on a shelf alongside a bunch of other boxes. Elite Trainer Boxes are perfectly designed in that way. 

But the per-pack price offered by these big boxes is hard to beat. Getting 36 packs of anything in a box is becoming more and more of a rarity in TCGs, and even at the current presale Market Price of $240, these work out to a great deal.

Three-Pack Blister

Contents: 

  • 3 booster packs.
  • Seel promo card.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $36.
  • Price per pack: $12.

These are the products you're most likely to find in a big-box store, and while the per-pack prices on these aren't always the greatest, they come in at a lower price point and always make for great gifts.

The current Market Price of three-pack blisters is hanging between $35-40 on live presale listings, giving us a per-pack price of around $12.

There will also be some number of retailer-specific blister products released, such as the Target-exclusive Xerneas and Keldeo Blisters that will come with a single pack and a promo of the named Pokémon.

Single-Pack Blister

Contents:

  • 1 booster pack.
  • 1 coin.
  • 1 promo card.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $20.
  • Price per pack: $20.

The basic item: the single-pack blister. So what is the price of a single loose blister pack, the kind that you'll see as stocking stuffers here in a few short months?

As of this writing, there are hundreds available on TCGplayer right at $20. Obviously this is the most expensive way to procure booster packs of the set to open, but it's very helpful to know the baseline that all the other products are working backwards from. Plus, now you know what's a fair price if you see one of these at a store!

Booster Bundle

Contents:

  • 6 booster packs.

Price:

  • Current Market Price (Oct 22): $66.
  • Price per pack: $11.

Coming in again at right around that $11 per-pack price point, the Booster Bundles are one of the premier mid-tier product releases for every set, and Delta Reign is no different. The Booster Bundles are a no-frills, pack-heavy release, and for that reason are quite popular with collectors looking to chase that Mega Rayquaza ex. 

All in all, Delta Reign has some giant shoes to fill following on the heels of 30th Celebration. It's a good thing that Mega Rayquaza is more than up to the task, and with Prerelease events starting up this weekend on Oct. 24, the time to officially move into the Pokémon TCG's third decade is here!
